newsitem.title: CHINA: Wild handover party rages in HK's expat hotspots.
newsitem.headline: Wild handover party rages in HK's expat hotspots.

text.p: Thousands of boisterous expatriates roamed Hong Kong's hot nightspot area of Lan Kwai Fong through the night to usher in a new era under Chinese rule with cheers, drinks and dancing.

Electrified crowds, crammed shoulder to shoulder with local Chinese who also frequent mainly yuppie haunts, waved Union Jacks, the red flag of China and the red and white bauhinia flag of Hong Kong as Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule at midnight (1600 GMT) on Monday.
"I've been waiting for six months for tonight," said Kenji, a 25-year old Japanese expatriate who has been working in Hong Kong for six months.
"Tonight is special. It is like New Year's eve," he said.

Charged with excitement, British women wearing Chinese-style cheongsam dresses, men sporting Chinese-style jackets and others wearing reversible hats with the Union Jack on one side and the Chinese flag on the other, raised their arms in the air, one after the other, to form a wave through narrow L-shaped streets.
Television screens showed the handover ceremony at the convention centre live.

As heir to the British throne Prince Charles ended a lavish tribute to the Hong Kong people before handing the bustling outpost of 6.4 million people back to China, balloons were sent floating skyward to a loud chorus of cheers and whistles.
People pumped their fists into the air as the crowd, sprayed with beer and in a wild, jubilant moment, chanted "Hong Kong, Hong Kong".
British men rushed to kiss Chinese women and shook hands with their local counterparts.
"We're in China now," said one expatriate who had watched the final moments of British rule tick away on a clock outside the popular Post 1997 restaurant.
One local Chinese hugged his friends. "I'm very happy," he said. "Hong Kong has returned to China. China is the motherland. We have come back!" he shouted.
As the official handover ceremony ended, and Governor Chris Patten sailed away on the royal yacht Britannia, the party went on in Lan Kwai Fong towards the dawn of a new era.
One expatriate who has lived in the territory for 20 years said Lan Kwai Fong had never experienced such a festive night.
"Lan Kwai Fong has never been as salubrious as this evening with the spirit of festivities and positiveness," he said.
Police kept a watchful eye on the crowd in Lan Kwai Fong -- the site of a crush on New Year's Eve in 1992 that left 21 people dead -- but no incidents were reproted.

It was business as usual in the girlie bars and expatriate drinking dens of Wan Chai, once a notorious red light district but in recent years better known as a haunt for tourists looking for a taste of the seedier side of Hong Kong's night life.

Despite fears that unruly elements among British expatriates and Hong Kong Chinese might cause disturbances, the overall atmosphere was unexpectedly placid. Wan Chai police said the streets were "peaceful".
Wan Chai's reputation as a red light area began in the 1940s and was made famous by Richard Mason's 1950s novel "The World of Suzie Wong", whose heroine was a Wan Chai prostitute.
